Jinny Lu placed second in 2025. (Kent Porter / The Press Democrat) By Charles Swanson | charles.swanson@pressdemocrat.com | The Press Democrat PUBLISHED: August 21, 2026 at 12:56 PM PDT | UPDATED: August 21, 2026 at 1:14 PM PDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Jinny Lu, a 6-year-old pug from Ukiah by way of Los Angeles and South Korea, took her unconventional beauty to a national stage this week following her victory at the 2026 World’s Ugliest Dog Contest . After being crowned the champion Friday, Aug.14, at the Sonoma County Fair in Santa Rosa, the celebrated rescue dog and her owner, Michelle Grady, traveled to New York City for a featured appearance Monday morning, Aug. 17, on NBC’s “Today” show. “It was a complete whirlwind, but joyful,” said Grady, who runs the Pug Hotel senior dog sanctuary in Ukiah . “In what lifetime did I ever expect this to happen?” During the broadcast, “Today” anchors Craig Melvin, Sheinelle Jones and Carson Daly, along with correspondents Dylan Dreyer, Savannah Sellers and Gadi Schwartz, fawned over Jinny Lu’s adorable hanging tongue and penchant for drooling. Schwartz, who was one of the judges at Friday’s contest, had traveled to Santa Rosa with his family to cover the competition. Grady also unveiled Jinny Lu’s latest necklace, commemorating her win after three previous appearances in the contest. Ukiah pug Jinny Lu, 2026 World’s Ugliest Dog Contest winner, and her owner Michelle Grady of The Pug Hotel senior dog sanctuary, join the cast of the “Today” show during a broadcast at NBC’s studio in Manhattan, Monday, Aug. 17, 2026. (Michelle Grady) "Today" show correspondent Gadi Schwartz — who traveled to Santa Rosa with his family to cover the 2026 World’s Ugliest Dog Contest — holds winner Jinny Lu backstage at NBC's studios in Manhattan before the Ukiah pug and owner Michelle Grady appeared on the show, Monday morning, Aug. 17, 2026. (Michelle Grady) Ukiah pug Jinny Lu, the 2026 World’s Ugliest Dog Contest winner, checks herself in the mirror backstage before her featured appearance on NBC’s “Today” show, Monday Aug. 17, 2026, in New York City. (Michelle Grady) Grady said she never expected her beloved pug to win, but attributes Jinny Lu’s victory to her personality. “She’s got her silly tongue, but I feel like it’s more the way she looks into people’s eyes,” Grady said. “She genuinely wants to be held by people, and different people.” Jinny Lu appeared to enjoy her newfound fame. She loved the crowds at Friday’s competition and embraced the attention in New York, where she and Grady saw “The Outsiders” on Broadway, walked around Times Square and met fans who recognized her on the street and asked to hold her for photographs. Ukiah pug Jinny Lu, the 2026 World’s Ugliest Dog Contest winner, explores Manhattan, Sunday, Aug. 16, during a trip to New York City for a featured appearance on NBC’s “Today” show on Monday morning. (Michelle Grady) “Every five steps, we were stopped because somebody wanted their picture taken with Jinny Lu, and that’s before the ‘Today’ show (broadcast),” Grady said. “I couldn’t have been more stunned that Jinny was famous.” The attention is a long way from Jinny Lu’s beginnings. Four years ago, volunteers with Pug Rescue of Korea rescued her from a small wooden box in South Korea. Grady later adopted her through the Los Angeles-based rescue organization. “I took one look at her and said, ‘That’s my pug,’” Grady said. “And I’m forever grateful because she’s such an important part of our grumble.” Jinny Lu, the 2026 World’s Ugliest Dog Contest winner, at the Pug Hotel senior dog sanctuary in Ukiah. (Michelle Grady) Jinny Lu, center, cuddles with fellow pugs at the Pug Hotel senior dog sanctuary in Ukiah. (Michelle Grady) As the contest winner, Jinny Lu received $5,000 in prize money, which is being donated to the Pug Hotel to help the nonprofit provide sanctuary for senior pugs and to rehabilitate, foster and rehome pugs in need, Grady said. Jinny Lu will also appear on limited-edition cans of MUG Root Beer, which sponsored the contest. When she’s not competing, Jinny Lu serves as an ambassador for the Pug Hotel, which Grady relocated from Rohnert Park to Ukiah in April. She frequently visits elementary schools with Grady to teach children about pet rescue and visits hospice patients and people in memory care facilities. “These pugs are so healing,” Grady said. “When you hold Jinny Lu, it just sort of lowers your heart rate.” The World’s Ugliest Dog Contest, a nearly 50-year tradition produced by the Sonoma-Marin Agricultural Association, celebrates dogs’ individual quirks and imperfections while promoting rescue and adoption. At this year’s competition, Jinny Lu beat eight other contestants, including dogs from as far away as Poland, to take the title. “This event has always been about celebrating the dogs that might otherwise be overlooked,” Mandy Clendenen, CEO of the Sonoma-Marin Agricultural Association, said in an Aug. 15 news release. For Jinny Lu, though, the national spotlight appears to be just another opportunity to do what she has always done best: make people want to pick her up. And, apparently, take her picture. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/mar.text: After an aggressive rate-cut cycle, the Indian fixed-income market could be entering a very different phase, with rising crude oil prices, elevated global bond yields and sticky inflation putting renewed pressure on the domestic bond market.Puneet Pal, Head of Fixed Income at PGIM India Mutual Fund, believes the rate-cut cycle is over and the Reserve Bank of India could be at the cusp of a rate-hiking cycle. He expects policy rates to rise by 50-75 basis points by the end of FY27, with bond yields likely to inch higher as inflationary pressures build.Yet, Pal believes rising yields could also create an opportunity for fixed-income investors over the next six months. With the 10-year government bond yield around 7%, he recommends a phased approach to investing, particularly in high-quality corporate bond funds and target-maturity funds.In this edition of ETMarkets Smart Talk, Pal discusses the outlook for interest rates and bond yields, the key risks for fixed-income investors, and how investors should position their portfolios as India moves from rate cuts towards a potentially tighter monetary policy cycle. Edited Excerpts -Q) With the US Fed back in a rate-hiking cycle and the Indian 10-year yield around 7%, how should investors rethink the fixed-income opportunity in India right now?A) Rising crude oil prices and elevated global bond yields are likely to keep the Indian bond curve under pressure. The CPI inflation projections in the last MPC policy meant that real rates would be negative for three quarters and with the current surge in crude prices, it’s very likely that CPI inflation projections will be revised higher, which , in our view, means that MPC will need to start hiking rates from October Policy onwards.We expect a 50-75 bps hike in policy rates by the end of FY27. The best time to invest in Fixed Income is when rate s and yields are rising and we think that the rise in yields will present a good investment opportunity for investors over the next six months.Q) The RBI has already delivered significant rate cuts, while inflation is moving higher. Do you think the easy part of the Indian bond rally is behind us, or can bond yields still move lower from here?A) The rate cutting cycle is over and we are at the cusp of a rate hiking cycle and as such we do not foresee any meaningful downside in yields from here.Indian bond yields have been rising since last year and the current deluge of liquidity on back of the FCNR flows can, at best, provide temporary relief to the bond markets. As the rate hiking cycle in India starts, we expect yields to gradually inch higher.Q) For retail investors looking to invest in Indian bonds today, how should they choose between government securities, high-quality corporate bonds, target-maturity funds and short-duration funds in this environment?A) Investors should invest basis their investment horizon and risk appetite and in the current stage of the interest rate cycle we would recommend high quality corporate bond funds and target maturity funds.Q) For an investor entering the bond market today, does a 7%+ yield on government securities offer an attractive entry point, or is there a risk of yields moving even higher?A) The current yields provide an attractive investment opportunity for fixed income investments though given the current uncertain geopolitical environment amidst elevated global bond yields and rising commodity prices, in our view, its better for investors to stagger their investments.There is a definite risk of bond yields continuing to trend higher as central banks hike policy rates and investors can continue to invest in a phased mannerQ) For Indian Bond Investors, What Is The Bigger Risk Today: Rising Inflation, Higher Us Yields, Or A Weaker Rupee?A) All the three risks are interlinked but Inflation is the biggest challenge for Fixed Income and thus monitoring Inflation is non-negotiable for fixed income investors.(Disclaimer: Recommendations, suggestions, views, and opinions given by experts are their own. These do not represent the views of the Economic Times.)

https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/vladimir-.text: James Knuckey Updated Sun, October 4, 2026 at 10:24 AM UTC 3 Vladimir Putin is ramping up the threats against NATO (Image: Getty) Vladimir Putin is rattling the nuclear sabre harder than ever - and it's time for Andy Burnham to stop beating around the bush on defence . Just a day after the Prime Minister stayed eerie silent on defence in his Labour Party conference speech, the Kremlin took tensions up a notch. In a "non-paper" memo to NATO , Moscow said it's ready to use its "entire arsenal" , including nuclear weapons , if the alliance threatened its Kaliningrad exclave. The document, it is reported, accused NATO of being on a "dangerous and reckless course". It also warned of "high risks" of direct armed conflict. Andy Burnham made little mention of defence in his Labour Party conference speech (Image: Getty) NATO denied the claims in the strongest possible terms , condemning the threats as "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric". But why did Russia do this? Was it to scare NATO? Or yet another attempt to weaken support for Ukraine ? Or perhaps it was to lay the foundations of a pretext for some kind of action against NATO? We will likely never know but one thing's for sure, Mr Burnham's silence on defence is increasingly deafening. He spent a grand total of around 40 seconds speaking about the issue in his Labour Party conference speech which lasted more than an hour. Much of it was focused on greater public control and NHS-style social care, funded by scrapping the triple lock . Russia is increasing its threats to NATO (Image: Getty) But none of these announcements mean anything unless our security is ironclad. After all, it is defence that underpins a nation's prosperity. The PM's words on the issue were the bare minimum of what we should expect. He promised the country will be "more able to meet" its NATO obligations, show leadership on the international stage, as well as "steadfast" support for Ukraine and standing up to threats "wherever they come from". What we learned about Mr Burnham's defence vision from this could be written on the back of a stamp - in other words, nothing. It's particularly disappointing after he indicated he would use the speech to finally lay out the roadmap to spending 3% and 3.5% of GDP on defence. This will, of course, take some tricky decisions, but in Mr Burnham's own words: "Change will be difficult. It always is." And as the old saying goes, there's no time like the present as Russia grows ever more brazen. Tensions are continuing to rise along NATO's eastern flank. Estonian authorities said an arson attack on a defence company providing military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage, commissioned by Russian security services. It comes after Germany blamed Moscow for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport , as well as repeated warnings of rising Russian sabotage and hybrid attacks. Moscow denied any involvement in both incidents. Meanwhile, Lithuania and Poland are working on evacuation plans together in the event of a Russian assault. Preparations were carried out earlier this week as part of major drills in Lithuania. Britain's newest attack submarine has departed its shipyard in Barrow-in-Furness, Cumbria, for sea trials. HMS Agamemnon will be put through a series of tests ahead of joining active service with the Royal Navy . 'Awesome Aggie' is the sixth boat in the Astute-class - the largest and most advanced submarines ever operated by the Senior Service - and her progress towards commissioning will be welcome news for Navy commanders. HMS Agamemnon has sailed for sea trials (Image: Andrew Linnett/MoD/PA Wire) The Astute-class has suffered from repeated availability issues over the years, with periods when none of the five in-service boats have been at sea. The submarines are nuclear powered but conventionally armed, capable of firing Spearfish torpedoes and Tomahawk land attack missiles. https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-v.text: To read the full Q&A with Laura Codruța Kövesi, click here . ATHENS — Ursula von der Leyen has not yet provided an in-person statement to the European Public Prosecutor's Office for its investigation into the procurement of coronavirus vaccines, according to an individual involved in the effort who was granted anonymity to speak freely. In 2024, EPPO took over the Belgian-led probe into alleged criminal wrongdoing in connection with vaccine negotiations between the European Commission chief and Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla. Prosecutors have been investigating von der Leyen for "interference in public functions, destruction of SMS, corruption and conflict of interest," according to legal documents seen by POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement Asked to respond to the assertion that von der Leyen has failed to provide a statement on the so-called Pfizergate affair, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said: "The Commission has demonstrably cooperated extensively with EPPO to clarify facts and assess events." "This was always done on behalf of and with the full support of the President. The President has always been, and continues to be, very cooperative in answering to any open questions — within the limits of her duties and her availability as President of the Commission.” In an interview with POLITICO, EPPO chief prosecutor Laura Codruța Kövesi, who wraps up her seven-year tenure on Friday, said she has on multiple occasions dealt with EU officials who refused to answer summons from her office. “Some politicians think that they are above the law,” she said. “If you are called in for a statement, you have to come.” She added: "I will not be shy to tell you that especially when important people are involved in the investigation — be it high-profile politicians or rich people who are connected to the political class, we have difficulties in exercising our competence." When asked whether von der Leyen was one of the officials in question, Kövesi said she wouldn't comment on specific investigations. Killing EPPO softly EPPO, set up in 2017 and operational since 2021, is tasked with rooting out crimes involving EU funds. As head of the organization, Kövesi said she has faced repeated attacks and attempts to undermine the institution and its work. Advertisement Advertisement “As I leave my office, I think of this famous Danish TV show, Borgen. There is a very famous saying there: 'In Brussels, no one can hear you scream,' and unfortunately, this is true," she said, in a nod to the Ridley Scott blockbuster Alien. "I am concerned that the EPPO is going to be killed softly because it's doing its job." Kövesi cited three main factors undermining the institution's work: chronic underfunding, delays in the revision of the organization's legal framework and the complexity of its bureaucratic architecture, which she said leads to "endless discussion about how to complicate the life of the prosecutors." Asked what she would do differently if she could start over again, the chief prosecutor said she “would do the same things, but maybe the others should change their behavior," adding that the biggest challenge her successor, German prosecutor Andrés Ritter, will face is keeping EPPO “independent and credible.” Greece’s 'blatant' intimidation Kövesi said that during her tenure, “the most blatant attempt" to intimidate EPPO prosecutors was in Greece, which was hit by a farm funding scandal last year — leading to the resignation of ministers and deputy ministers. The cases of four MPs from the ruling New Democracy party are currently being heard in court. They all plead innocent. Last May, EPPO sent a formal complaint to the Commission regarding moves by the Greek government to block EU prosecutors from investigating Greek lawmakers. It also complained about the Greek Supreme Judicial Council’s refusal to renew the mandate of European-delegated prosecutors for five years at EPPO's request. Kövesi warned that this could result in EU funding cuts for Greece under Article 16 of the EPPO Regulation. The cooperation between EPPO and the Greek government has been difficult, with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis hinting at a political agenda by EPPO by complaining of "selective leaks." Advertisement Advertisement “All the noise was created to blame EPPO that we play politics instead of discussing what happened in reality,” said Kövesi. “Some politicians speak about an independent and efficient judiciary, until you touch them and until you go close to their inner circle. In that moment, the prosecutors are abusive, they have a political agenda, they are not needed.” Some Greek government officials have suggested that Greece could simply opt out of the EU institution, but Kövesi said this is “almost impossible.” The chief prosecutor also raised concerns about the impact of budgetary restrictions on EPPO's work elsewhere in the bloc. The organization is currently setting up its operations in Hungary, which officially became a participating member of EPPO in August 2026 — but Kövesi is skeptical about how successful it will be. “We explained exactly what we need to do our job, but the Commission proposed half of [the budget] we need,” she said, adding that EPPO's "credibility is at stake" in countries like Poland, where "expectations were huge" but the organization has not been able to deliver on its promises. EPPO is also investigating the alleged misuse of more than €4 million by the Identity and Democracy group, a defunct political grouping in the European Parliament whose debts Patriots for Europe could be forced to repay. The latter group includes France’s far-right National Rally, led by Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner ahead of France's 2027 presidential elections. “If you ask EPPO to abstain and to not do anything because there are elections in Europe, we will not work at all,” said Kövesi. Mari Eccles contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement
